files.text:
By a low lamp

The kings of Assyria wrote on their walls. Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt Kalhu on the Tigris, the mound now called Nimrud, and moved his court there around 879 BCE. He lined the rooms of his new palace with slabs of gypsum carved in low relief: the king with his bowl and his bow, attendants with daggers and fly-whisks, winged spirits with a bucket of holy water. Across every slab, straight through the robes and the beards, the masons cut the same text: his names and his titles, his wars, the building of the palace, over and over, room after room. Scholars call it the Standard Inscription. It was not put there to be read so much as to be there, like a name woven into the hem of a cloth.

A scribe in Babylon wrote with a reed. He cut the end square, or nearly, pressed its corner into a pad of damp clay held in the other hand, and lifted it out again. That was a wedge, and the wedge was the whole of the alphabet: every sign was a small cluster of them, upright, lying down, slanting, or a hook made with the corner alone, and a practised hand could set down three or four a second without looking, turning the tablet a little at the end of each line. Children learned it the same way, on round tablets the size of a palm like this one. The teacher wrote a line, the pupil copied it underneath, and the clay, as long as it had not been fired, could always be wetted, smoothed with the thumb and written on again.

That is why so much of it is lost, and why so much survives. A tablet dried in the sun is only hard mud, and rain or a damp floor will take it back. The ones that last are very often the ones that burned. When the Medes and the Babylonians sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE, the palace fell in on the library of Ashurbanipal, and the fire that ended the Assyrian empire baked thousands of its tablets hard under the rubble, where Layard’s diggers found them in the winter of 1850. Ebla, Mari, Ugarit: the archives we can read are, more often than not, the ones somebody’s enemies set alight.

Under the soft, even light of a museum, worn carving goes flat. A wedge is a small three-sided pit, and in light from everywhere at once each face is as bright as the next, so the sign dissolves into the grain of the clay. The people who read these things carry a lamp, or wait for the sun to go low, and hold the light nearly level with the surface and move it. Now one face of every wedge catches the light and another falls into black; each sign becomes a little constellation of bright and dark triangles, and a line that could not be seen a moment ago can be read from across the room. Turn the lamp and other marks come up. A stroke that runs along the light disappears and a stroke across it leaps out, so the reader turns it again, and again, and writes down what all the lights agree on.

Reflectance transformation imaging does the same thing with a camera. The tablet is fixed beneath it and photographed forty or fifty times, each time lit by a flash from a different point on an imaginary dome above, and the software works out, for every pixel, how its brightness changes as the light moves, and so how the surface there is turned. Afterwards anyone can sit at a screen and draw a virtual lamp across a tablet in London or Philadelphia, often more legibly than in the hand, and signs that defeated generations of readers have come up out of the clay this way. This page does it with one photograph and a good deal of guesswork: the shape of each object was estimated from the way the studio light fell on it, then the studio light was taken away, and your hand put in its place.

# raking-light A carved surface relit by a low lamp. Epigraphers read worn inscriptions and cuneiform by raking light: a lamp held nearly level with the surface and moved around it, so every wedge and chisel cut throws a shadow and the marks leap out. Here the pointer is that lamp (on a phone, the tilt of the phone and a sideways drag), and a single museum photograph becomes a surface: a clay tablet lying on the page throws its own long shadow across the paper and the words, and the wedges of the script turn into small triangles of light and black that change as the lamp goes round. ```html ``` Or `import { rakingLight } from './raking-light.js'` and call `rakingLight(figure, options)`; it returns `destroy()`. The `` is the plain photograph and sets the size. It is what shows without JS or WebGL, in print, and until the maps arrive. Each figure fetches its maps only when it comes within 800 px of the viewport. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-normal` | `normal` | required | the normal/height map (PNG, lossless): r g = surface normal, b = height | | `data-albedo` | `albedo` | required | the photo with its own studio light divided out (alpha = the cut-out) | | `data-height` | `height` | `20` | the full range of the height channel, in texels of the map. Printed by the processing step | | `data-kind` | `kind` | `object` | `object`: a cut-out lying on the page; the canvas reaches past it (up to its own size each side, never past the page's sides) for the shadow it throws on the paper. `surface`: a rectangle, no cast shadow | | `data-material` | `material` | `clay` | `clay` (matte, faint sheen) or `stone` (a little more polish) | | `data-light` | `light` | `-45 12` | where the lamp rests: azimuth and elevation in degrees. Azimuth is on the screen: `0` = from the top, `-90` = from the left, so `-45` rakes from the upper left | | `data-cast` | `cast` | `0.6` | 0-1, how dark the shadow on the paper is | | `data-relief` | `relief` | `1` | scales the heights (longer or shorter shadows) | | `data-muted` | `muted` | `0.2` | 0-1, how far the colour of the object is muted toward grey | | `data-reach` | `reach` | `6` | in object radii: past this distance the pointer stops being this object's lamp and the lamp drifts back to rest | | `data-ambient` | `ambient` | `1` | scales the room's light. The demo's band uses `.5`: a dark room, so the lamp does the work | | `data-falloff` | `falloff` | `2` | surfaces only: how fast the lamp's light dies across the band, `exp(falloff × along - .35)` with `along` = ±1 at the ends. The demo uses `4.4`: about 3× in brightness between the lamp's end and the far end at 25% | The options object wins over the attributes. ## How the lamp moves - **Desktop:** the pointer is the lamp. Its direction from the object's centre is the lamp's azimuth; its distance sets the elevation, from 21° when it is over the object down to 6° a couple of radii away. Near the very centre the lamp keeps the side it was on. Far away (past `reach`) it drifts back to rest. Leave the window and it goes back to rest. For a band, "radius" is half its height, so sweeping along the band runs the lamp low, high, low. - **Phone:** turning the phone left or right swings the lamp up to ±100° round the object; tipping it toward you lowers it (`tilt.js`, shared, smoothed, its level drifting back over about 12 s). A sideways drag on any piece turns the lamp too (260° across the screen); a vertical swipe scrolls the page as usual (`touch-action: pan-y`). Six and a half seconds after the last touch the drag is let go and the lamp returns. - **Keyboard:** each piece is focusable. Left and right arrows walk the lamp round by 20°, up and down raise and lower it by 3°; Escape sends it back. - **Always low.** The elevation is clamped to 5°-25°. A frontal light would just give back the flat photograph. - **A hand-held lamp.** It follows through a critically damped spring (`STIFF = 6.5`/s): a little lag, no overshoot, settled in about a second. ## How it works **Offline (Python), from one evenly lit photograph:** 1. **Cut-out** (objects): a chroma threshold against the studio backdrop seeds GrabCut, the largest component is kept and its holes filled, the outline is smoothed and pulled in 2 px, and the alpha is a signed distance with about a pixel of anti-aliasing. 2. **Large form:** Depth Anything V2 Small (`depth-anything/Depth-Anything-V2-Small-hf`, run locally through `transformers`) at about 1000-1400 px. Its output is smoothed past its 14 px patch grid (which otherwise shows as faint stripes under grazing light); for the wall the camera's perspective lean (a fitted plane) and the slowest swell are taken out. This gives the relief figures standing off the ground and the pillow of a tablet. 3. **Fine carving:** soft frontal light leaves the bottom of every cut darker than the open surface, so *dark is deep*. Log-luminance is band-passed at four scales (differences of Gaussians, 0.7-18 px) with per-object weights (the round tablet's wedges are big, so its finest bands are turned down; the fragment's script is fine, so they stay up). A soft knee keeps one dark crack from becoming a canyon, and **shrinkage** (soft-thresholding at 28-45% of the 95th percentile) throws away faint mottle (stains, grain, sensor noise) that would otherwise read as orange peel under a low light, while strong marks keep their depth. Then **isolated blobs are taken out**: a grey closing by a line segment at 8 angles, keeping the minimum, fills any dark spot shorter than the segment whichever way it lies, while a carved stroke survives along its own direction (bright specks likewise, by opening). Segment 11 px for the round tablet (its pits are stains, not writing), 9 for the relief (the dressed stone between the figures reads smooth), 5 for the fine-script fragment. What is taken out of the height stays in the albedo, as a stain. 4. **Objects get a rim:** the height rolls down to the paper over about 7% of the object's size. The rim is built from a heavily blurred alpha, not a distance transform (whose staircase becomes a saw-tooth in the normals), and eased out so the dome has no knee. 5. **Normals** from the combined height (Sobel), and the height itself in the blue channel, normalised; its range in texels is the `data-height` value. 6. **Albedo:** the photo's own lighting is fitted (ambient + one soft light from the upper left against the recovered normals, least squares) and divided out (to the 0.85 power, so it is not flattened lifeless), with a broad correction for uneven studio light; a cavity term from the height divides out the occlusion that soft light leaves in pits, since the shader's shadows will put it back. At a cut-out's rim the colour is carried out from just inside, so a steep, badly explained edge cannot fringe. Map sizes are about 1.3 texels per device pixel at DPR 2 for the tablets and 0.85-1 for the band. Normal maps are PNG; lossy compression would show as blocks under raking light. **In the shader (one full-screen pass per piece, only while the lamp moves):** - **Diffuse:** `albedo × (ambient + lamp × (1 - e^(-1.25x)))`, with `x = N·L × shadow × falloff × 1.3 / sin(elevation)`: exposed for a low lamp, so flat clay under it reads near its own colour, faces turned to the lamp glow, and faces turned away fall to a dim, slightly cool ambient. A shoulder above 0.8 keeps the glow from clipping. - **Shadows:** 26 steps of a height-field ray toward the lamp, growing geometrically from 0.6 to about 240 texels, so a wedge's own wall and a raised figure's long shadow both come from the same march. The penumbra widens with distance (a lamp has a size). Interleaved-gradient jitter on the first step turns step banding into fine grain. A shadow keeps 14% of the lamp (light back off the walls), and a **bounce** term proportional to the local lamp strength keeps grooves at the lit end dark rather than black, while the far end of a band still falls toward the dim ambient. - **Falloff:** the lamp is a hand-held one, close. On an object, an inverse square from a point a little off its near edge; on a wall, exponential along the light (`data-falloff`), so the end of the room away from the lamp falls into shadow and the whole brightness gradient flips when the lamp moves: measured on the demo band at 25%, 2.5-3.1× between the lamp's quarter and the far quarter. - **Sheen:** a faint Blinn-Phong highlight (clay 0.05 at 14, stone 0.1 at 34). - **Shadow on the paper** (objects): the object's silhouette, softened (drawn at a quarter size and scaled up), is its height above the paper, about a sixth of its size. Each paper pixel looks toward the lamp (14 steps) for the steepest angle up to the object's top and compares it with the lamp's own elevation across the lamp's disc (13° wide): near the object the angle is steep and the shadow is dark and sharp; further out it sinks toward the lamp's height and the shadow thins and softens. Five dithered taps across the light widen its sides the same way. The room's light fills it in with distance, and it is followed out to about the object's own size, then fades to nothing. A narrow contact shadow grounds the edge from every side. - Premultiplied output on a transparent canvas, so the cut-out's anti-aliased edge and the shadow composite cleanly over the page. WebGL2 where available (mipmapped maps, so an object drawn smaller than its maps keeps a clean edge); WebGL1 otherwise. ## Tuning - In the processing: `FORM` (how tall the large form stands, px) and `DETAIL` (how deep the carving reads), the band weights, and the shrinkage. Too much detail or too little shrinkage gives a crumpled, gritty surface; too little and the marks go soft. Look at three lamp positions side by side before choosing. - In the shader: `uExpo` (exposure for a low lamp), the falloff (`fall`), the shadow penumbra (`.1 * t + 1.1`), `uAmb`, `uLamp` (about 3400 K), and `MATERIALS`. `uThick` and `uCastLen` set the shadow on the paper. - `STIFF` sets the lamp's lag. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--rl-ground` | `--paper-2` | behind a surface while it loads | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | The lamp and the room are not themed: the lamp is warm, the room dim. On a dark page the shadow on the paper (near-black ink) will barely show; it is meant for paper. ## Behaviour and cost - **Nothing runs when the lamp is still.** The loop runs only while the lamp moves (pointer, drag, tilt, the spring settling) and stops once it has settled; off screen, in a hidden tab, or idle, nothing runs. Verified: 0 frames in 2 s idle; a pointer move costs about 1.5 s of frames. On a phone held still the lamp still eases slowly home as `tilt.js` re-levels (about 12 s), then stops. - Canvas DPR capped at 2. A full-width band on a 1440 px screen is about 3.4 Mpx a frame, 28 texture reads a pixel: fine on a laptop GPU while moving. An object's canvas is up to 3× its size each way (room for its shadow); its paper pixels cost 70 small texture reads while the lamp moves. - **Weight:** the maps are the cost. The tablets: about 0.3 MB albedo + 0.8-0.9 MB normal each. The relief band: 0.8 MB albedo + 2.4 MB normal (2400 × 977, lossless). They load only as each piece nears the viewport. - Without WebGL, `createImageBitmap`, or if a map fails to load, the `` stays. If the GPU drops the context, the img shows until it comes back. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The images are decorative (`alt=""`, `aria-hidden`); the canvas is `aria-hidden` and never takes input. Each piece is focusable with a default `aria-label` ("A carved surface under a low lamp. Arrow keys move the lamp around it.") unless you set your own; focus shows an accent ring. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: the lamp rests raking from the upper left (the finished, beautiful state). Hovering does nothing and the phone's tilt is ignored; only a deliberate act moves it: pressing on a piece and dragging (mouse or finger), or the arrow keys. It then moves **instantly**, with no easing and no return to rest: direct manipulation, nothing animating by itself. - Text under a cast shadow keeps its contrast (the shadow is at most about 35%). - Print shows the plain photographs. ## Credits - Photographs: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0): a student exercise tablet (Old Babylonian, 321878), a commentary on *Enuma Anu Enlil* (321874), and a relief panel from the Northwest Palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud (photograph DP-346-001, via the Met's Wikimedia Commons donation). Details in `assets/credits.json`. - Depth: Depth Anything V2 Small (Yang et al., 2024; Apache-2.0), run offline; nothing of it ships. - After the practice of raking-light photography and reflectance transformation imaging (Malzbender et al., HP Labs, 2001; Cultural Heritage Imaging). No third-party code in the component.
